overview: This bill raises the maximum size of government-backed loans available to small manufacturers through the Small Business Administration (SBA), the federal agency that guarantees loans made by private lenders to small businesses. It defines a small manufacturer as a small business whose main work is manufacturing and whose production facilities are all in the United States. For these businesses, it raises the cap on the SBA's main 7(a) loan program to as much as $10 million, raises the export-loan cap from $5 million to $10 million, and raises the limit on certain 504 loans (long-term loans for equipment and real estate) from $5.5 million to $10 million. The SBA's inspector general (its internal watchdog) would study whether the larger loans default more often or add costs to programs meant to operate at no cost to taxpayers, and the SBA would report for five years on jobs created or kept by the larger loans. A Senate committee approved the bill on July 29, 2025, and held a hearing on May 13, 2026.
for: Supporters say manufacturing equipment and facilities are expensive, and higher loan limits would help small U.S. factories grow and keep production at home, with reporting built in to track risks and job results.
against: Critics say larger loans concentrate more government-backed risk in fewer borrowers, which could raise losses or fees in programs meant to run at no cost to taxpayers.
